planting.note: Set divisions in early spring into dry-mesic, humus-rich woodland soil under deciduous canopy; established clumps handle root competition and dry shade under mature oaks better than most sedges.

directions: Long-stalked sedge is one of the earliest woodland plants to flower each year, sending up small purplish-anthered spikes on wiry stalks while deciduous trees are still bare, often alongside the first spring ephemerals. Its low tufts of narrow leaves have a distinctive maroon-tinged base and slowly expand into loose colonies via short rhizomes, favoring the dry slopes and upland oak-hickory woods where it is naturally found. Because it is adapted to dry shade and duff-covered soil, it needs little supplemental water once established and pairs well with trout lily, sessile bellwort, and other early spring woodland natives. Leave old foliage in place through winter since it stays semi-evergreen and provides some of the season's first green color.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in dappled to full shade; it forms a well-mannered clump rather than spreading, so it can be tucked among ferns and wildflowers without crowding them.

directions: Graceful sedge earns its name from slender, thread-like peduncles that arch and droop under the weight of its narrow seed spikes, creating a soft, weeping fountain effect distinct from stiffer upright sedges. It is among the most widespread woodland sedges of eastern deciduous forests, forming loose, non-aggressive clumps of fine bright-green foliage that stay tidy for years without dividing. Its fine texture makes it a natural companion for broader-leaved woodland perennials like wild ginger or hostas, adding contrast without competing for space. A light cutback of old foliage in late winter keeps new spring growth looking fresh.

planting.note: Set divisions in spring into dry-to-mesic, well-drained woodland soil, ideally with some limestone influence; established clumps tolerate summer dry spells in deep shade better than most fine-leaved sedges.

directions: Hairy sedge is one of only a handful of North American sedges with distinctly fuzzy, soft-pubescent leaf blades and seed capsules, giving its foliage a velvety texture unlike the smooth or glossy leaves of most woodland relatives. It forms a loose, upright clump of broad leaves reminiscent of plantain-leaved sedge but with a noticeably softer, hairier feel when touched. Native to dry-mesic upland forests, often over limestone, it is a good textural choice for a shaded rock garden or dry woodland edge where showier sedges struggle. It needs minimal care beyond an annual tidy of spent foliage in late winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into rich, moist woodland soil in dappled shade; it tolerates the disturbed edges and semi-open understory of regenerating woodlots better than many fussier sedges.

directions: Bur-reed sedge produces small, tightly clustered, globe-shaped flower spikes strung along the upper stem that resemble miniature burs, a distinctive silhouette that sets it apart from sedges with more open or drooping seed heads. Its stiffly upright, sharply triangular stems form dense clumps in the rich, semi-shaded woodland edges and floodplain terraces where it naturally grows, making it a sturdy choice for a taller layer in a shaded native planting. It is more tolerant of disturbed soil and part-sun conditions than many strict woodland-interior sedges, so it adapts well to newly planted or regenerating shade gardens. Cut back old growth in late winter before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Plant plugs 10-14 inches apart in spring into dry-mesic, humus-rich upland soil in shade; it colonizes by short rhizomes to knit into a loose groundcover under mature trees.

directions: Fibrous-rooted sedge is one of the first sedges to green up each spring, its slender leaves emerging while overhead trees are still leafless, and it slowly knits together into loose colonies through a dense mat of wiry roots that gave the species its common name. It naturally carpets dry-mesic oak-hickory woodlands and tolerates root competition and seasonal drought better than many fine-textured groundcover sedges, making it a practical no-mow substitute for lawn under established shade trees. It stays low and non-aggressive compared to running species, so it can be combined with taller ferns and spring wildflowers without overtaking them. An occasional tidy of old foliage in late winter is the only maintenance it needs.

planting.note: Set divisions in spring into rich, moist-to-dry-mesic woodland soil, ideally with limestone influence, in full to partial shade; clumps establish slowly but need little attention once rooted in.

directions: Hitchcock's sedge belongs to the same broad-leaved group as plantain-leaved sedge but is distinguished by its finely hairy seed capsules and leaf sheaths, giving close-up textural interest that smoother relatives lack. It forms a modest, slow-spreading clump of wide, arching, deep-green leaves well suited to the rich, calcium-rich woodland soils it favors in the wild. Because it stays compact and non-aggressive, it works well as an accent among ferns, wild ginger, and spring ephemerals in a shaded limestone-influenced garden bed. Established plantings tolerate brief dry spells but perform best with consistent woodland-floor moisture.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in dappled to full shade; it prefers the cooler microclimates of north-facing slopes and moist ravines over hot, dry sites.

directions: Drooping wood sedge produces slender, arching stalks that bow gracefully under dark, blackish-scaled seed spikes, giving the plant a somber, elegant look distinct from the paler-scaled sedges it otherwise resembles. It is more at home in the cool, moist ravines and north-facing slopes of northern and Appalachian forests than in warmer, drier woodland sites, so it rewards gardeners with consistently shaded, humus-rich soil. Loose tufted clumps increase gradually without becoming weedy, making it a good textural filler beneath ferns and taller woodland wildflowers. Trim back old foliage in late winter to keep clumps looking fresh as new growth emerges.
